title: PDAI Structured-XML OCR System
text:
0.1 Two trees, one collection
A PDAI collection is not a pile of PDFs. It is a folder of documents plus a small set of files that say what belongs here, how each document is identified, and what grammar its pages must obey. Those files are the metadata. Without them the pages can still be read; they cannot be cited, scoped, or checked.
Code and data are separate on purpose. The workspace at ~/ai-mac-studio/pdai/collections/<name>/ holds schemas, scripts and instructions. The documents themselves live on the PDAI-1 volume at /Volumes/PDAI-1/pdai-collections/<name>/. Nothing in the code tree holds page images; nothing on the volume is the place to invent a schema.
The volume folder is what this chapter describes. It has two layers.
The folder name of a document is its citation key. Bischoff2004/ produces @book{Bischoff2004, …}. That is the join the search stack uses; renaming the folder without rebuilding the bib breaks it.

medieval-sec is Bischoff’s Katalog der festländischen Handschriften des neunten Jahrhunderts — three volumes, nothing else. This is the folder as it stands on PDAI-1.

├── volumes.yaml
├── bibliography.yaml

├── page.dtd
├── catalogue.dtd
├── entry_schema.yaml
├── status.json               overall: not_ready

├── Bischoff2004/             Teil II: LAON – PADERBORN, 2004

diaries uses the same layout with different names (tablet.dtd instead of catalogue.dtd, ten ADART volumes instead of three Bischoff volumes). The files change; the jobs do not.

title: PDAI Structured-XML OCR System
text:
0.3 The plan
volumes.yaml is the collection plan. It answers one question: which documents belong here, and how is each one processed? It does not describe the printed record — that is the schema — and it does not carry bibliographic fields. A document that is not in the plan is not in the collection.

The three Bischoff volumes, as the plan states them.
collection: medieval-sec
collection_root: /Volumes/PDAI-1/pdai-collections/medieval-sec

volumes:
  - id: Bischoff1998
    volume: I
    teil: "AACHEN – LAMBACH"
    route: scan
    content: catalogue
    pages: 518
    source: /Volumes/PDAI-1/pdf_sortiert/bischof/Band_I_Einzelseiten.pdf
id is the folder name. route and content tell the pipeline what kind of pages to expect. source is the PDF the folder was harvested from — a provenance pointer, not a second copy of the book.

diaries adds split: true for volumes photographed as two-page spreads. That is a plan fact: it changes how pages are rendered, not what a tablet is.

text:
0.5 The two DTDs
A formalised edition prints structured records inside running text. Those records span page breaks, so the collection carries two grammars, not one.









File
Governs
May do
Must not do




page.dtd
one OCR’d page
record what is printed here, as complete or cut blocks
infer a number, a heading, or a field from another page


<record>.dtd
the assembled record
join a block cut at the bottom of one page to the block cut at the top of the next
invent a field the pages never printed




medieval-secdiaries


The record is a catalogue entry. catalogue.dtd groups entries under a <libraryplace> and lets <shelfmark> repeat, because a manuscript dispersed across libraries is printed as a chain joined by +.
page.dtd          →  <page> of <entryblock> elements
catalogue.dtd     →  <catalogue> of <libraryplace> / <entry>


The record is a tablet edition. tablet.dtd on the collection (and in config/) covers both the page and the assembled <tablets> document.
page.dtd          →  <page> of diary / comments / calendar blocks
tablet.dtd        →  <tablets> of <tablet> records



Both DTDs sit on the collection as well as in the code tree, so a page XML file can name them without reaching back into ~/ai-mac-studio. pdai-config.json records the paths under schema_ref.
The schema YAML (entry_schema.yaml / tablet_schema.yaml) is the prose behind the DTD: every element cites the printed page it came from. How that schema is derived, and why it is written before production OCR, is the schema-first method.

title: PDAI Structured-XML OCR System
text:
0.6 The stylesheet pair
A page.dtd can only be rendered meaningfully if the viewer knows how each element should look. The rendering convention is therefore a pair:
collections/<name>/config/   page.dtd  +  page.css    authored here
/Volumes/PDAI-1/pdai-collections/<name>/  page.dtd + page.css    deployed here
Both files of the pair are wrappers of the shared page language (Chapter 2): the collection page.dtd includes page.dtd v4.0 and pdai-core.mod, and the collection page.css is an overlay on the shared book sheet. The deployed page.dtd is a flattened, generated copy.

0.6.1 How it works
Schema rendering is always on. pdai_server.py injects the shared sheets (pdai-page.css, pdai-epistolary.css, pdai-astronomical.css, pdai-translation.css, pdai-receipt.css), the renderer repro-xml.js and window.PDAI_SCHEMA_RENDER = true into every viewer page, and adds the collection’s page.css (served at GET /api/collection/{collection}/page.css) as the last sheet when the collection has one. A collection without page.css is rendered by the shared sheets alone.
The renderer (ReproXML) parses the page XML with DOMParser(…, 'text/xml'), so empty DTD elements (<witness/>, <row/>, <date/>) survive as empty nodes. Every element becomes an HTML element with data-el="tagname" and each XML attribute as data-<attribute> (data-type, data-side …); a marginal also carries data-kind (marker or note), which the margin rules of pdai-page.css use.

The base rules covering elements common to every DTD (page, header, p, hi, table, figure, footnotes, …) live in ai-viewer/config/styles/pdai-page.css. Collection-specific rules override and extend that base.


0.6.3 Coverage tool
ai-viewer/scripts/css_coverage.py parses the DTD and the collection CSS and reports any element or enum value with no rule. It exits non-zero on a gap and accepts --scaffold to emit a starter stylesheet:
# Verify coverage
python scripts/css_coverage.py ../collections/diaries/config

# Generate a skeleton for a new collection
python scripts/css_coverage.py ../collections/new-collection/config --scaffold > page.css
Run the coverage check whenever the DTD gains a new element or attribute.


0.6.4 Iron rule: DTD and stylesheet authored together
A new page DTD must have a matching page.css before the collection enters production OCR. The coverage check enforces this at CI time. Unstyled elements render as anonymous <div> blocks, which is not an error — but they will never look correct. Author the two files in the same session and commit them together.

title: PDAI Structured-XML OCR System
text:
0.7 What is not metadata
Pages, OCR XML, structure.xml, the lemma index, the stanza database and the Chroma store are products. They are absent or incomplete on a collection that is not_ready, and that is a processing fact, not a metadata gap. status.json reports those products. It does not replace the plan.
status.json is written by the collection contract audit. Correcting a document count after a volume is removed is honest; claiming the collection is ready because the bib now validates is not.

title: PDAI Structured-XML OCR System
text:
0.8 The -prim/-sec collection convention
When a collection contains both primary sources and secondary literature, split them into two separate collection folders on PDAI-1:

<name> — primary sources (correspondence originals, critical editions of the author’s own works, archival documents)
<name>-sec — secondary literature (Jahrbücher, monographs, Festschriften, research volumes about the person/topic)

Both are served by the same edition viewer and appear under the same edition in editions.yaml. The split uses ditto — never symlinks.
# Example: Pirckheimer
pirckheimer/         # Willibald Pirckheimers Briefwechsel (7 vols., Beck)
pirckheimer-sec/     # Pirckheimer-Jahrbuch, edited volumes, secondary scholarship
Why split? Different material classes → different OCR templates → different DTDs. A printed scholarly journal must never be transcribed with a letter template. The -sec split makes the classification boundary explicit in the data structure itself, so ai-classifypdf prepare <collection> can apply the right profile per collection without any guesswork.
Existing examples: kepler-prim/kepler-sec, copernicus-prim/copernicus-sec, waefler-prim/waefler-sec, euler_sec, pirckheimer/pirckheimer-sec.
config/ artifact set (per collection, in pdai/collections/<name>/config/):







artifact
purpose




collection_profile.yaml
OCR run plan: class, template, DTDs, run_approved


ocr_classification.json
per-document classification result + evidence


bibliography.yaml
verified title-page records with _provenance


volumes.yaml
collection manifest: which documents belong, what type



These are produced by ai-classifypdf prepare <collection> (the preparation step) and consumed by OCR automatically. They are the PDAI equivalent of “metadata before data”.

title: PDAI Structured-XML OCR System
text:
0.9 Iron rules






WarningSix constraints that keep the layout honest




The plan is the membership list. A bib entry without a folder, or a folder without a plan row, is a defect. Do not leave either standing.
biblio.xml is sourced, never guessed. Title page and imprint only. bib_build will not invent the missing year.
Folder name = bib key = biblabel. Three spellings of the same identity, kept identical.
The page DTD does not assemble records. Cross-page join is the record DTD’s job, and only after the pages exist.
Classification precedes OCR. Run ai-classifypdf prepare <collection> before any production OCR. Never hand-pin a template in pdai-config.json without an ocr_classification.json that documents why.
Pilot gate for book-sized documents (> 50 pages). For large documents, never launch full batch processing directly. Draw a 5-page random sample, execute pilot OCR, and audit against DTD/audit rules/facsimile. If defects emerge, run the improvement loop (prompt overlay, normalizer regex, document-specific page.css) until 100% PASS before batch unlocking.



The production commands that fill pages/ are in the pipeline skill. This chapter stops at the folder that those commands write into.

2.1 The layers
One grammar core, one prompt composer, one margin stylesheet, one letter assembler.
Every PDAI page, whatever its collection, is written in one page language. A collection may add elements, margin types and measures of its own; it cannot rename or drop a word of the common vocabulary. The same vocabulary is read by the OCR prompt, the normalizer, the audit and the viewer, from one file.

A collection grammar is a wrapper. It sets the entities it needs and declares only what the canonical page lacks; the first declaration of an entity or an attribute wins, so the overrides come before the include:
Deployment writes a flattened copy of each grammar to the collection root on PDAI-1 (python -m ocr_runner.page_language deploy --collection <c>), with a GENERATED header that names the source files and their hash, so no reader resolves relative includes across volumes.
Measured. The restructuring was checked against every page XML on PDAI-1 (python -m ocr_runner.page_language census): of 159,170 pages, 93,279 were valid against their grammar before and 95,751 after; no document lost a valid page (2,444 documents compared). Reports: pipeline/ocr-runner/reports/page-language/census-{before,after}.json.

title: 2  The page language
text:
2.2 Margins






NoteThe marginal



Everything printed in a margin of the page is a <marginal side="…" type="…">. It stands directly before the first word of the printed line it is printed beside, inside that paragraph, whichever margin it is in. Beside a table row it is a child of that <tr> — first for the left margin, last for the right — and the viewer draws it as a gutter cell of the row. side is the margin where it is printed.


The type is one word of a closed list. The list and its split are parameter entities of the core, so the prompt, the audit and the viewer read the same words:








Kind
Type
Printed as




marker
line-number
printed line count (5, 10, 15 …)


marker
folio
manuscript folio or page of an earlier print (22v, Bl. 14)


marker
symbol
a sign (cross, dagger, hand)


note
topic
the author’s or editor’s marginal gloss or lemma


note
reference
a cross-reference or source citation in the margin


note
date
a date printed in the margin



note, marginal-note, label and gloss are forbidden aliases; the shared normalizer maps them to topic, maps an untyped numeral to line-number, and maps <note place="margin…"> of archival prompts to <marginal type="topic">. An untyped prose marginal stays untyped, because the page does not say whether it is a gloss or a reference. Collection extension types are declared by their wrapper, with their gloss in the wrapper’s comment: doc-id (KGW 19) and entry-number (medieval-sec).

2.2.1 Display
The viewer renders a marginal as an inline span with data-side and data-kind (marker or note). pdai-page.css sets it position: absolute with no top, so it keeps the height of its own line and moves sideways into the margin. The sheet reserves a margin only on a side that carries marginals — a narrow marker gutter, a note column, or both, markers outermost. A post-render pass in repro-xml.js pushes a marginal down when it would overlap the previous one on the same side, and lets the sheet grow when a long note runs below the last paragraph. Notes are unboxed.
A collection page.css sets only the measures (--pdai-note-width, --pdai-note-gap, --pdai-marker-gutter) and the typography of its types; pdai-coherence reports any rule that redeclares position, display, float or offsets of a margin (COH-CSS-MARGIN-GEOMETRY).

The line count 45 stands in the right margin of the first line, Kepler’s gloss on Brahe in the left margin beside Denique eadem, the line count 10 in the right margin of the first line of Etsi igitur.

text:
2.4 Partitur control
Every page a runner saves carries the partitur that produced it:
<meta partitur="kepler-ocr@3f400c0df6fa" layers="page-language,base,qwen38"
      overlay="kepler-ocr.qwen38.j2" engine="qwen3.8:27b-mlx" model="qwen3.8:27b-mlx" …/>
partitur is the family prefix and the first twelve hex digits of the SHA-256 of the composed instruction with the page variables left as placeholders, so it is the same for every page of a model and volume and changes with any layer.
pdai-partitur check --collection kepler-prim     # per model: layers, hash, missing overlays, lint
pdai-partitur census --collection kepler-prim --write-status
check exits non-zero when a model of the chain composes base-only or an overlay fails the lint (grammar declared in an overlay, a margin type outside the DTD). census counts, per document, the pages per model and partitur and merges them into status.json (ocr_partitur); legacy pages count under legacy:<instruction_template>. pdai-audit --all runs the census.
State on 2026-09-28: check reports four models without an engine overlay — gemini-3.8-flash on medieval-sec and karman-nachlass, kimi and gemini-3.8-flash on kepleriana-munich-2024. They compose base-only until an overlay is measured.

text:
2.5 Content control and dual read
A partitur tells an engine what to write; it cannot tell anyone whether the engine did. For that the pipeline keeps an independent witness of every page: Apple Vision (fastimage --mode ocr, on device, about 0.5 s per page, no API cost) reads the scan into lines with their geometry. Vision structures nothing and misses signs such as †, but it is reliable about where text stands. ocr_runner.content_control turns that reading into a census:

Vision reads KGW’s old-style figures as letters (“1o”, “4o”, “so”, “2°”, “390»”); a token counts as a margin number when it hangs into the margin, and is then read as 10, 40, 50, 20, 390v. The line counts of a page form one series; a reading outside it (“3720” for the folio 372v) is kept as uncertain and never inserted. When more than a quarter of the lines open with a number (a register), the page is a list and has no margin census. A figure zone must hold ink outside the boxes of the text lines, so the blank beside an indented address or signature block is not a figure.
check(xml, census) measures a reading against it (missing, extra and misanchored margin items, flat tables, figures without zones, notes the scan does not print); repair_margins anchors margin numbers at the first word of their line, places a row’s number in its <tr>, moves a sign to the unread mark on its side, corrects the type (a sign is a symbol, a number that is not a line count is a folio) and removes notes and paragraphs the scan does not print; crop_figures cuts the zones out of the scan as page_NNN_fig_K.png when their number equals the number of <figure>s. What the census cannot read it reports and never fills: an italic folio that Vision and both engines misread stays a mark_unread gap.
python -m ocr_runner.dual_read runs two engines on the same page, each under its own composed partitur, and scores both readings with the audit, the text-validity check against Vision (schema_audit.text_validity) and the content check. It lists where the two readings diverge — margin items, tables, figures, notes, and the word windows in which they disagree, each with the reading Vision supports — takes the better one (structure score plus half a point for every divergent window in which Vision supports the other reading; a text gap that resembles the transcription character by character is Vision misreading Fraktur, not lost text), repairs it, sets printed-page from the census, and writes only with --write (the old page is kept as page_NNN.xml.v<n>). Reports go to collections/<c>/quality/dual-read/<doc>/page_NNN.json; --reuse re-measures saved readings after a change of the repairs without calling an engine; --escalate 3 runs the second engine only when the first reading, repaired, still scores 3 or more.

title: 3  Layered OCR, and the Kirch reprocess
text:
3.1 One page, two prompts
The page grammar, the prompt, and the model are three separate decisions. Kirch was processed as if they were one.
A page is tagged in the universal page language. The prompt that asks for those tags is built in layers, and each layer is stamped on the page. The model is chosen after that prompt exists, from a measurement on a real page. Kirch has none of the three: its pages were read in August 2026 by gemini-3.6-flash and qwen3.5:cloud, from templates that name elements page.dtd v4.0 does not admit.
The grammar itself is the page language. This chapter is what changed in the prompt and the model choice, and what that implies for Kirch.
KGW 3, printed page 102, was read twice on 28 September 2026. The facsimile has a running header 102, line counts 45 and 10 in the right margin, and a gloss on Brahe in the left margin beside Denique eadem.
The first prompt was the older Kepler overlay, handed to the model as a single file. Kimi returned the gloss with type="marginal-note", which is not a word of the margin list, and it missed the printed header. Qwen3.8 returned the gloss as type="note". Gemini 3.8, on that same older file, returned XML that failed to parse. qwen3.5:cloud answered HTTP 410. deepseek-v4-pro:cloud answered HTTP 400: the model does not accept an image.
The second prompt was composed. ocr_runner.cure_config.compose stacks five layers, and stops at the last one that exists:
Kimi then ran as kepler-ocr@739ec396938e with layers page-language, base, kimi. Gemini 3.8 ran as kepler-ocr@ef4f29445dd4 with page-language, base, gemini38. Both returned the header 102, both line counts as line-number on the right, and the gloss as type="topic" on the left. The audit reported 0 defects and 0 blockers. The hash is the first twelve hex digits of the composed instruction, with the page variables left as placeholders. It is the same for every page of one model and volume, and it changes when any layer changes. pdai-partitur check refuses a model that composes base-only or whose overlay names a tag outside the grammar.
Local qwen3.8:27b-mlx remains the engine for harvest and for a run that must stay on this machine. Rapid-MLX (rapid-mlx/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit-MTP-MLX, prefill step 8192, vision cap 800,000 pixels, thinking off, one request in flight) is a route for that same model. On this page it was legal and slower, and it dropped a line count the composed cloud prompts kept. It is a measured option for a local pilot, and the printed-page default stays kimi-k2.7-code:cloud, with gemini-3.8-flash only when Kimi fails on that page.

text:
3.3 How Kirch is reprocessed
The reprocess follows the document-grammar procedure: profile, grammar, layer, fit, run. Nothing is written to a volume before its gate passes.
Grammar per document. Each of the 17 documents has a document_profile.yaml that names its page classes (kalendarium, computus, entry, table, register-table, facsimile-text, inset-facsimile, show-through, and the default) and a wrapper DTD that adds only what the front matter attests. The Vision classifier assigns a class to each page (three votes, gemini-3.5-flash-lite); the geometry census breaks ties.
Layer per engine and class. The prompt is composed from the page language, the collection base, the volume layer, the engine overlay, and the class layer. Layers were trained on 46 pilot pages spread over all 17 documents.
Fit check. Every reading is compared with its facsimile by measurement only: DTD and audit, table rows and columns against the image census, text agreement with the Vision reading (Antiqua) or between two engine readings (Fraktur, mixed), figures, margins, and ink share (a leaf without ink must yield an empty <main/>). A page fits when no finding fails.

title: 4  One grammar per document
text:
4.1 What the profile establishes
A collection is a set of documents, and its documents differ in format. The grammar, the prompt layer and the model are therefore fixed per document, in a fixed order, and each step is measured before the next begins.
Until version 1.1 of the Partitur pilot-gated-ocr-pipeline, a document took the grammar of its collection. That holds where the volumes of a collection share one format (the volumes of one critical edition). It fails where they do not: within the collection Kirch, the Forschungsberichte are modern prose, the Handbuch is a sequence of articles with fixed rubrics, and the Kalenderreihen are calendars whose pages are tables in two colours. Version 1.2 makes the document the unit.
The profile of a document (config/volumes/<doc>/document_profile.yaml, skill document-profile) records three things, each with an evidence grade.
The grades are those of the schema-first method: front-matter (stated in the edition), facsimile-only (observed, provisional), unattested (neither). A vocabulary item graded unattested is not declared in the grammar.
Page OCR remains page-scoped. Entry types are the input of a separate segmentation pass that assembles records across pages; they do not change what one page reading contains.

text:
4.5 Model selection
The engine of the full run is the best measured engine among those with a passed layer: quality first, then latency, then cost. The measurements come from the Model Assessment Hub (ma_best_model), and each pilot run is recorded with ma_record_run. The default is kimi-k2.7-code:cloud; gemini-3.8-flash with thinking off runs only for a page on which Kimi failed. A different default is reported to the owner and is not adopted without confirmation.

4.6 Registered contract
The stages profile-document, derive-document-grammar, fit-check and select-model are registered in partitur_register.duckdb under the goal path pipeline/ocr/pilot-gated, with the result specification and verification of each stage (production pipeline). The former stage improvement-loop is now train-layer.

title: 5  The Production Pipeline
text:
5.1 What this chapter covers
This chapter describes the single, authoritative production pipeline that takes an incoming PDF or scan and delivers a certified, queryable PDAI document to the ai-viewer endpoint. The pipeline is unified: one pilot-gated-ocr-pipeline Partitur (v1.1.0), one pdai-audit engine, one learning loop. The per-collection forking that characterised earlier iterations is deprecated; this is the canonical path.
flowchart LR
  delivery["PDF or scan delivery"] --> ingest["ingest and classify\nai-classifypdf"]
  ingest --> profile["schema derivation\ndocument profile"]
  profile --> pilot["pilot gate\n5-page sample"]
  pilot --> ocr["schema-first OCR batch\nqwen3.8:27b-mlx"]
  ocr --> certify["certify-and-learn\npdai-audit --all"]
  certify --> learn["learning loop\nannotations A/B"]
  learn -. "regression gate" .-> ocr
  certify --> complete["corpus completion\nstanza · lemma · gazetteer · lexicon"]
  complete --> register["readiness manifest\nedition registry"]
  register --> viewer["ai-viewer endpoint"]
Every arrow corresponds to a concrete command or service. Every node corresponds to a system component described below.

title: 5  The Production Pipeline
text:
5.2 Stage 1: Ingest and classify
Command: ai-classifypdf ingest --collection <name> or ai-classifypdf prepare <collection> followed by ai-classifypdf run.
What happens: The PDF is harvested into the collection folder on PDAI-1, page images are extracted at 300 DPI, and the document is classified into one of the recognised document-class templates: printed-scholarly, special-script, handwritten-archival, or catalogue. The preparation step produces ocr_classification.json and collection_profile.yaml — the plan the OCR stage reads.
Engines: - fastapple backbone (Apple fastimage + Ollama vision LLM) for highspeed ingest; kimi-k2.7-code:cloud is the structuring model. - Classic ai-scholar process path (kimi-k2.7-code:cloud, per-page fallback gemini-3.8-flash) remains available via --classic.
Output: pages/page_NNN/ folder tree under /Volumes/PDAI-1/pdai-collections/<collection>/<doc>/, with one PNG per page and pdai-config.json recording the harvest provenance.






ImportantClassification precedes OCR



Never begin production OCR without a completed ocr_classification.json. The template, DTD, and model are all determined here; guessing them inline is not permitted.

title: 5  The Production Pipeline
text:
5.3 Stage 2: Schema derivation
Command: ai-classifypdf prepare <collection> (also produced in Stage 1 for standard collections; for formalised editions, a dedicated schema-derive skill).
For formalised editions — catalogues, letter registers, ephemerides — the schema derivation reads the printed front matter of the volume and derives the record schema before any OCR. The derivation produces:

config/page.dtd — grammar for one OCR’d page
config/<record>.dtd — grammar for the assembled record
config/audit_rules.yaml — declarative cue and vocabulary rules
config/page.css — collection overlay on the shared book sheet: measures (--pdai-note-width, --pdai-marker-gutter) and typography; margin geometry is shared (Chapter 2)

The derivation is never retrospective: the DTD is written before the first production page is processed. Evidence grades: front-matter (authoritative), facsimile-only (provisional), unattested (do not invent).

title: 5  The Production Pipeline
text:
5.4 Stage 3: Pilot gate
Command: python3 scripts/pilot_gate.py --vol <vol> or via the Partitur stage draw-pilot-sample + execute-pilot-ocr + audit-structural-gate.
Iron rule: For any document with more than 50 pages, the pilot gate is mandatory before batch OCR is unlocked. Five pages are drawn randomly, OCR’d under the assumed DTD, and audited in three passes:

DTD validation — the XML must be well-formed and valid.
audit_rules.yaml — vocabulary, cue, and SCH-* checks.
Visual facsimile comparison — every VIS-* class checked against the actual scan.

If any blocker is raised, the improvement loop runs before batch unlock.

5.5 Stage 4: Schema-first OCR batch
Command: python3 scripts/<collection>_ocr_run.py --vol <vol> (or chain_<collection>.sh for multi-volume succession).
Primary model: qwen3.8:27b-mlx (Ollama local, M1 Ultra, think=false, image scale 0.5, num_ctx=8192, 1 worker — optimal on this hardware). Fallback: kimi-k2.7-code:cloud. Special-script / handwritten: kimi-k2.7-code:cloud directly.
Every page is processed against the collection config/page.dtd, rendered by ai-viewer at the collection’s dedicated port, and logged to a JSONL telemetry file under /Volumes/PDAI-1/tmp/<collection>-ocr/<vol>.jsonl. The live monitor is available at http://localhost:<port>/ocr-monitor?volume=<vol>.

Command:

5.6.2 The tag hierarchy protocol
Every page in the volume is logged as a content-free structural fingerprint: tag names, nesting, and structural attributes only — no transcription content. Each page receives a SHA-256 hash of its pure S-expression. This creates the zero-regression anchor: when a prompt overlay or normalizer is updated, diff_tag_protocols() compares structural hashes in under 50 ms across all pages, catching any lost table, corrupted equation, or newly introduced element instantly.


5.6.3 Figure completion census
Every <figure> element is audited for:

@ref attribute (required)
<caption> element (printed caption, if present in the facsimile)
<description> element (rich geometric or diagrammatic description)

Completion rates are expressed as four states: complete_full (caption + description), complete_desc (description only, standard when no printed caption exists), caption_only, and empty. Target: 100% of figures at complete_full or complete_desc.


5.6.4 The four-layer fault model
Every assembled fault case is attributed to one of four root-cause layers:

System

5.6.5 The learning bridge (--emit-annotations)
Every assembled fault case is posted to the ai-query server (POST /api/annotations, port 5113) as an ocr-audit annotation, carrying: the fault’s collection, volume, and page coordinates; the observed defect (full FaultCase dataclass); the targeted fix directive; and the regression prevention anchor. The payload is also persisted as quality/<vol>/learning_annotations_payload.json.
Once annotations are registered, the A/B-gated instruction learning loop is triggered via POST /api/learn/from-annotations. The loop proposes a patch to the responsible SKILL.md (Layer 1–2) or schema file (Layer 4), runs the golden test set before and after, and promotes the patch only when the pass rate improves with no regression. This is an iron rule: no ad-hoc fixes to generation errors of a Partitur — all corrections go through the versioned learning system.







NoteRepairing a produced collection



When certification finds defects in a collection that is already produced, the repair follows the cure method: diagnosis, attribution to a layer, a remedy tested on 3–5 specimen pages, application to the flagged pages only. See Improving collections.

text:
5.10 Steering catalog
pdai/collections/ocr_catalog.yaml is the one file that maps every collection to its Partitur, model, ports, data roots, and DTD class. The pdai-audit CLI reads this catalog automatically so metadata (viewer port, model identities, edition label, volume titles) is always derived from the catalog rather than hardcoded in audit scripts.






WarningOne audit engine, one entry point



pdai-audit --collection <c> --vol <v> --all is the only supported way to run a comprehensive audit. The per-collection scripts/audit_check.py files are deprecated forwarding shims — they inject --collection <c> and call schema_audit.cli.main. They continue to work for backward compatibility but should not be maintained further.
pdai-audit is the console script of the schema-audit package at pipeline/schema-audit/. The corpus-readiness audit of ai-lemma-index (status.json) is a separate command, pdai-corpus-audit.

title: 6  Schema Architecture
text:
6.1 The canonical page DTD (v4.0) and its core
The canonical page grammar lives at pdai/pipeline/ai-scholar/src/ai_scholar/schemas/page.dtd. Since v4.0 it includes two modules shared by every PDAI grammar (Chapter 2):
Every content model of page.dtd is a parameter entity (page.content, main.content, p.content, hi.content, fn.model, header.model, footnotes.model, footnote.content …). The page variants (page_letter.dtd v4.2, page_section.dtd, page_annotated.dtd, page_translated.dtd) are wrappers of page.dtd; the record grammars (letter.dtd, section.dtd, parno.dtd, the collections’ tablet.dtd, catalogue.dtd and KGW 19’s document.dtd) include pdai-core.mod.

title: 6  Schema Architecture
text:
6.2 Layer 1: Generic ai-scholar stage chain
The ai-scholar processing pipeline produces pages against page.dtd. Its OCR templates carry the page-language fragment as a generated block (python -m ocr_runner.page_language sync-ai-scholar). This is the layer that enestroem, Euler and the other unprofiled collections use.

title: 6  Schema Architecture
text:
6.3 Layer 2: Collection wrappers
A collection with elements that have no canonical equivalent has a wrapper config/page.dtd: it sets the entities it needs, declares its own elements and attributes, and includes page.dtd. The first declaration of an entity or attribute wins, so the overrides stand before the include.






Important



A collection grammar adds to the page language. It never removes or renames a core element or margin type, and it does not declare record elements (cross-page assembly belongs to the record grammar). It may add margin types (marginal-type.extra), widen what a margin or a cell may contain (marginal.content, cell.content) and relax meta / figure requirements (meta.req, figure.ref.req).









Collection
Its own elements (beyond the page language)

running-header, letter-head / letter-closing families, section, lineno, fnmark, equation; KGW 19: document-entry, doc-*, margin type doc-id

The flattened copy that deployment writes to PDAI-1 is what the viewer host and external readers see; the audit validates against the sources.

title: 6  Schema Architecture
text:
6.4 The page / record split
A page DTD governs one physical page. Records assembled across two or more pages belong to a separate record DTD. This split keeps truncation visible: a page that begins mid-letter and ends mid-paragraph is valid XML against the page grammar; the assembler joins it (ocr_runner.assemble_letters for letters).
page_letter.dtd → one physical scan page (letter-part per letter on it)
letter.dtd      → one assembled letter from first to last page, <pb/> between pages
Never declare the record root element as a required top-level child of <page>. Use optional children so a page with an open record at top and bottom is still DTD-valid.

title: 6  Schema Architecture
text:
6.5 Versions
page.dtd v4.0, page_letter.dtd v4.2, letter.dtd v4.2, pdai-core.mod v1.0, pdai-table.mod v1.0 (schemas/registry.yml). Collection wrappers name the version of the grammar they wrap in their header comment; page XML names it in <meta output_schema="…">.

title: 6  Schema Architecture
text:
6.6 Agent-driven schema derivation
New collection schemas are derived by schema_derivation_agent (Partitur at development/ai-agent-orchestrator/agent-store/schema_derivation_agent/, registered at pipeline/ocr/schema-derive).
The agent has four stages:

locate-conventions — reads the edition’s front-matter statement of record form; stops if no declaration exists.
emit-record-schema — writes config/<record>_schema.yaml with status: front-matter | facsimile-only grades for every field.
verify-against-facsimile — checks the draft against 3–4 body pages and records corrections.
emit-dtds — generates the collection wrapper config/page.dtd (entity overrides + own elements + include of page.dtd) and config/<record>.dtd.

All four stage instructions are externalized as SKILL.md files under pdai/skills/pipeline/schema-derive/.

text:
7.3 Worked example: medieval-sec (Bischoff Katalog)
Front matter source: “Aufbau der Beschreibung”, pp. 5–6.
Bischoff’s Katalog explicitly declares the order of fields in each catalogue entry:

Ort · Bibliothek · Signatur — Inhalt — Datierung — Herkunft — Schrift — Literatur

Stage 1 extracts this declaration:
record_sections:
  - name: Ort
    order: 1
    xml_tag: ort
    content_type: text
    optional: false
    generated_from: "p. 5 col. 1, first field"
    status: front-matter
  - name: Bibliothek
    order: 2
    xml_tag: bibliothek
    content_type: text
    optional: false
    generated_from: "p. 5 col. 1"

title: 7  DTD Derivation Playbook
text:
7.4 Worked example: diaries (ADART Astronomical Diaries)
Front matter source: Introduction to ADART vol. I, pp. xxi–xxv.
The front matter describes the tablet structure (obverse/reverse, column structure, transliteration conventions). The template was derived accordingly.
Note that the diaries collection added repeat_penalty: 1.15 to the OCR options (via DIARIES_DELTA in diaries_ocr_run.py) because early transcriptions showed excessive repetition of Babylonian month names.

title: 7  DTD Derivation Playbook
text:
7.5 Worked example: kepler-prim (KGW)
Front matter source: KGW editorial introduction, and the Briefverzeichnis.
Kepler’s Gesammelte Werke is a mixed-content scholarly edition combining Latin and Early Modern German. The letter-head apparatus was not declared in one place but inferred from the consistent pattern across all letter pages. Fields derived from body observation rather than front matter carry status: facsimile-only.
The table ban documented in earlier KEpler collection READMEs was reversed by the 2025 schema-first approach: <table> is now required for all mathematical ephemerides and trigonometry grids.

title: 7  DTD Derivation Playbook
text:
7.6 CSS scaffolding after DTD generation
After emit-dtds completes, run css_coverage.py --scaffold to generate a starter page.css from the new DTD:
python3 pdai/pipeline/schema-audit/src/schema_audit/css_coverage.py \
  --dtd collections/<name>/config/page.dtd \
  --scaffold > collections/<name>/config/page.css
This produces a valid CSS with placeholder display rules for every declared element. Refine the visual rules against the facsimile using the visual-layout-audit skill.

8.2.2 <header>, <footer>

8.2.3 <p> (paragraph)
Main text paragraph. May contain: #PCDATA | hi | fn | marginal | equation | ref.
Never flatten a table or figure into <p>. A <p> is linear prose.


8.2.4 <hi> (typographic emphasis)
Attribute rend: closed vocabulary — italic, bold, spaced, smallcaps, superscript, subscript.
Missing rend is an audit violation (SCH-REND-MISSING). Never use <hi> without rend.


8.2.5 <marginal>
Everything printed in a margin (Chapter 2). A <marginal> stands directly before the first word of the printed line it is printed beside, inside that paragraph (or cell, or letter element).
Attributes (declared in pdai-core.mod; #IMPLIED in the grammar, required by the audit on pages produced by a composed partitur):







Attribute
Values




side
left, right — the margin where it is printed


type
markers line-number, folio, symbol; notes topic, reference, date; collection extensions doc-id (KGW 19), entry-number (medieval-sec)



note, marginal-note, label and gloss are not types; the normalizer maps them to topic. A marginal is never a <p> of its own and never the last thing in a paragraph.


8.2.6 <figure>
<figure ref="fig_057_1">
  <caption>Fig. 1: Epicycle diagram</caption>
  <description>Circle with inner circle, labeled P and O</description>
</figure>
Never replace a figure with an image crop. The <description> element is the text transcription of what the figure contains; <caption> is the printed label.


8.2.7 <table>, <tr>, <th>, <td>
Mathematical ephemerides, trigonometry grids, and data tables must be transcribed as genuine HTML-style table markup — never flattened to <p>. Column counts must be consistent across all <tr> within a <table>. Inline mathematics within cells uses LaTeX syntax ($formula$).


8.2.8 <equation>
Display-mode mathematical expression. Placed as a direct child of <page> or as a block child of <p> (the latter triggers a CSS layout violation that the coherence audit flags).
<equation display="true">$$\sin 30° = \frac{1}{2}$$</equation>


8.2.9 <footnotes>, <footnote>, <fn>
Footnotes always appear at the bottom of the page inside <footnotes>. <fn> is the inline superscript marker; <footnote> is the note entry.
<p>The comet appeared<fn>3</fn> on the 12th.</p>
<footnotes>
  <footnote><fn>3</fn> Observed by Kepler, KGW III p.~47.</footnote>
</footnotes>


8.2.10 Epistolary apparatus (kepler-prim, pirckheimer, karman-nachlass)
<letter-head> contains: <reference>, <date>, <archive>, <salutation>.
<letter-closing> contains: <greeting>, <signature>, <address>, <postscriptum>.
These elements are collection-specific extensions beyond canonical v3.0.

title: 8  Structured Page XML Reference
text:
8.4 Production rules

Page OCR is page-scoped. No cross-page inference. Assemble records in a separate segmentation pass after all pages are complete.
XML must be escaped for editorial angle brackets: use < / >.
<think> blocks and markdown fences from the model must be stripped by the normalizer (ocr_runner.normalize) before the XML is stored.
Ampersands must be escaped to & in all text content.
HTML tags (<b>, <i>, <sup>, <sub>, <br>) are forbidden in PDAI XML and trigger audit code SCH-HTML-TAG.

On an M1 Ultra running qwen3.8:27b-mlx, two concurrent Ollama requests share one model instance. The model is memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound.

title: 10  Audit Reference
text:
10.8 The tag hierarchy protocol
The tag hierarchy protocol provides a content-free structural fingerprint of each page for sub-50 ms regression testing after OCR improvements.
What is stored: For each page, the protocol logs the S-expression tree of XML tag names, nesting order, and structural attributes only — no transcription text. A SHA-256 hash of the S-expression serves as the page’s structural identity.
How regression testing works:
from schema_audit.tag_protocol import diff_tag_protocols
deltas = diff_tag_protocols(protocol_v1, protocol_v2)
# Returns per-page structural changes: gained/lost elements, depth shifts
A prompt overlay update that inadvertently drops all <table> elements will surface within 50 ms as a mass structural delta on table pages. A fix that correctly joins hyphenated words across <p> boundaries shows no structural change (the same elements remain, differently populated).
The protocol JSONL file is:
quality/<vol>/tag_hierarchy_protocol.jsonl
One JSON object per page, with fields pidx, sha256, depth_histogram, element_counts, and s_expr_truncated (first 512 chars of the S-expression).

@dataclass
class FaultCase:
    fault_id: str          # e.g. "FAULT-kgw15-p042-001"
    collection: str
    volume: str
    page: str              # pidx
    defect_code: str       # SYN-*, SCH-*, VIS-*, or composite
    fault_summary: str     # one sentence
    fault_description: str # precise description for the learning loop
    root_cause_layer: int  # 1=Prompt, 2=Normalizer, 3=CSS, 4=DTD
    root_cause_detail: str
    targeted_fix: dict     # {target_file, rule, regression_anchor}

The targeted fix names the file to patch and the rule to add or amend. The regression anchors are page indices that the fix must not break. Both fields are consumed by the learning loop when it proposes an instruction patch.

title: 10  Audit Reference
text:
10.11 The learning bridge (--emit-annotations)
When --emit-annotations is passed to pdai-audit, every FaultCase in the dossier is posted to the ai-query server as an ocr-audit annotation:
POST http://127.0.0.1:5113/api/annotations
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "phase": "ocr-audit",
  "subagent": "ocr:kepler-prim",
  "raw_query": "kepler-prim/kgw-15/p042",
  "observed": { ...FaultCase fields... },
  "comment": "[FAULT-kgw15-p042-001] Table flattened to <p> on p042 ...",
  "expected": "SCH-TABLE-FLAT rule: require <table> when | cue present",
  "instruction_ref": "config/kepler-ocr.qwen38.j2",
  "status": "open"
}
The payload is also persisted as quality/<vol>/learning_annotations_payload.json for traceability and offline re-ingestion when the server is unreachable.

10.11.1 What happens after posting
The ai-query annotation loop (port 5113, assessment.duckdb) receives the annotation and queues it for the A/B-gated learning pass:

POST /api/learn/from-annotations proposes a patch to the SKILL.md or schema file named in instruction_ref.
The patched instruction is stored as a new version in instruction_versions with status candidate.
The golden test suite is re-run with the patched instruction.
If the golden pass rate improves with no regression on the regression_anchors pages, the version is promoted to active.
If it does not improve, the candidate is rejected and kept in the registry for forensic purposes.

Iron rule: Every OCR defect that reaches the fault dossier must enter the annotation system and be addressed through the versioned learning loop. No ad-hoc fix to a prompt or normalizer is permitted outside this flow. Code-side probes are supporting signal only; the responsible SKILL.md is the patch target.

title: 10  Audit Reference
text:
10.12 audit_rules.yaml structure
Each collection maintains a config/audit_rules.yaml consumed by the shared Auditor class. The file has four sections:
syntax:
  strip_think: true      # <think> blocks → SYN-THINK-LEAK
  strip_fences: true     # ``` fences → SYN-FENCE
  validate_dtd: true     # DTD validation → SYN-DTD-FAIL

forbidden_tokens:
  - pattern: "<b>"
    code: SCH-HTML-TAG
    severity: repair
  - pattern: "&(?!amp;|lt;|gt;|apos;|quot;)"
    code: CHR-AMP-UNESCAPED
    severity: repair

vocabulary_rules:
  - element: hi
    attribute: rend
    allowed: [italic, bold, spaced, smallcaps, superscript, subscript]
    code: SCH-REND-UNKNOWN
    severity: repair
  - element: marginal            # the page-language vocabulary, read from the DTD
    attribute: type
    allowed: dtd                 # pdai-core.mod + the collection's marginal-type.extra
    require_on: partitur         # a missing @type is a defect on pages with <meta partitur>
    code: SCH-MARGINAL-TYPE
    severity: repair

cue_rules:
  - pattern: "\\|"        # pipe character often signals a table
    required_element: table
    code: SCH-CUE-MISSING
    severity: blocker

title: 10  Audit Reference
text:
10.13 Negative control requirement
Every audit_rules.yaml must be validated with a negative control test suite (test_audit_rules.py) that:

Injects each defect type deliberately into a known-good XML sample.
Asserts that the expected code is raised.
Asserts that no code is raised for the clean control.

python3 collections/<name>/scripts/test_audit_rules.py
# Expected: 10/10 PASS
A rule that does not trigger on a deliberately injected defect is not a rule.

title: 10  Audit Reference
section: 10.15 Composite scoring in the learning loop
text:
10.15 Composite scoring in the learning loop
The AuditEvaluator (development/ai-agent-orchestrator/src/orchestrator/learning/audit_evaluator.py) blends objective defect counts into the learning loop grade:
composite = llm_score × (1 − penalty)
penalty   = blocker_fraction × 0.5 + repair_fraction × 0.2
A promoted overlay must reduce measured blockers and repairs compared to the baseline, not merely win a self-assessment. The regression_anchors from the fault dossier are the exact pages that must show 0 blockers after promotion.

title: 10  Audit Reference
text:
10.16 Naming collision note
“Audit” appears in two places in the PDAI workspace:

pdai-audit (this document): the OCR quality engine in pipeline/schema-audit/ — structural, visual, figure, dossier, report, bridge.
pdai-complete status: the corpus-readiness audit in ai-lemma-index — checks whether OCR, stanza, lemma, gazetteer, and Chroma stages are complete.

They are orthogonal. pdai-audit is about transcription quality; pdai-complete is about corpus stage completion. Both write a status.json into their respective domains (quality/ and the collection root on PDAI-1).

11.1 What RELAX NG governs
The RELAX NG schema pdai-structure.rnc governs structure.xml, not page XML. It is orthogonal to the DTD system: page DTDs govern single OCR’d pages; RELAX NG governs the assembled document-level argumentative structure.
The two systems operate at different granularities:

title: 11  RELAX NG Layer
text:
11.2 Structure.xml
structure.xml is the PDAI document-level source of truth for running text organised by argumentative hierarchy. It is produced by the ai-scholar structure sub-app:
ai-scholar structure extract --doc-id E57
ai-scholar structure validate --doc-id E57
ai-scholar structure ingest --doc-id E57
The RELAX NG schema lives at format/lettre-pdai/src/lettre_pdai/schemas/pdai-structure.rnc.

title: 11  RELAX NG Layer
11  RELAX NG Layer
text:
11.4 RELAX NG vs DTD tradeoffs
PDAI uses DTDs for page and record grammars because: - DTD validation is available in all standard XML parsers (lxml, Python xml.etree) without additional dependencies. - OCR runners write XML and validate in the same process; DTD validation adds negligible overhead.
RELAX NG is used for structure.xml because: - structure.xml has interleaved content models that are inexpressible in DTD. - The <argument> / <evidence> relationship is context-dependent in ways that require RELAX NG’s interleave and choice operators. - structure.xml is produced by an AI agent, not directly by the OCR runner, so the validation toolchain (Jing, lxml relaxng) is already available.

title: 11  RELAX NG Layer
text:
11.5 Connection to ai-query
The structure.xml layer feeds into the ai-query artifact engine (proof-structure from structure.xml, D3 force graph, timeline, KWIC). When ai-query resolves a query about argumentative structure in an edition, it reads structure.xml through the pdai_document_agent sub-system.
The RELAX NG contract file is documented in format/lettre-pdai/docs/structure-contract.md (previously an unlinked file; it is now referenced from the main Quarto book index).

title: 12  The cure method
text:
12.1 Purpose
A PDAI collection that is already produced can still carry defects: lost footnotes, flattened tables, generation loops, apparatus entries filed as body text. The cure is the method for removing them. It differs from production in one respect: it never processes a collection as a whole. It measures, selects the defective pages, tests a remedy on a few of them, and applies it only where the measurement found the defect.
The method is written down in three places that state the same thing at different levels:

title: 12  The cure method
text:
12.4 Iteration budget and stop criterion
Every iteration runs within a page budget and a time budget, declared in the collection’s config/cure.yaml:
budget:
  pages_per_iteration: 40
  minutes_per_iteration: 90
  specimen_min: 3
  specimen_max: 5
The runner reports pages beyond the budget as deferred and does not process them. A pilot with deferred pages fails. An iteration whose target metric does not improve ends with a report of the measurement; it does not start another run of the same remedy. This rule answers the failure that gave rise to the method: a repair session on copernicus-prim ran for half a day because each unsatisfactory result started a new collection-wide run instead of a narrower test (see the Copernicus case).

title: 12  The cure method
section: 12.5 One processing agent at a time
text:
12.5 One processing agent at a time
Only one process that writes page XML or occupies the OCR engines runs at a time: the targeted re-OCR runner (ocr_runner.cure_run), the normalizer application (normalize_apply --apply), the overlay learning loop (ocr_runner.cure_learn) or a production run (ai-scholar process). On the M1 Ultra a second request to qwen3.8:27b-mlx saturates the GPU; it does not double throughput. The gate and apply ops of the Partitur refuse to start while another such process is live.

13.1 Stage 0 — Scope
The scope fixes what an iteration may touch. It reads three sources:

13.2 Stage 1 — Diagnose
Two measurements run per scope. Both are deterministic.

13.2.1 Text validity
pdai-validity --collection <c>              # all documents

Vision results are cached per image modification time; a rerun compares only the XML again and takes seconds for the 3,644 pages of copernicus-prim.

14.1 Why attribution comes first
A repair removes a defect class only if it changes the layer that produced it. A normalizer cannot restore text that the engine never transcribed; a new OCR pass cannot correct a DTD that forbids a structure the source prints. The attribution assigns each class one layer before any remedy is chosen.

.venv/bin/python -m ocr_runner.normalize_apply --collection <c> --doc <d> --specimen 127,347,553
# re-OCR or overlay: pilot tree under <tmp>/pilot/<d>/<stamp>/
.venv/bin/python -m ocr_runner.cure_run --collection <c> --doc <d> --pilot --sample 5 --also 127,347,553
The two gates check different properties.







Gate
A specimen page passes when




normalizer (normalize_apply --specimen)
the rule changes the page (a no-op fails), the result is well-formed, applying the rule again changes nothing (idempotent), and the word sequence is preserved except for rejoined hyphenations


re-OCR and overlay (cure_run --pilot)
the best engine answer reaches verdict ok without a reject code (LOOP-REP, TRUNC, SYN-WELLFORMED), or the current XML is already valid and is kept; no page is deferred by the budget



The normalizer gate stores for every passed page the hash of the source XML and the structural_hash of the result in <data>/quality/<d>_norm_gate.json. --apply refuses when the gate is missing, belongs to another normalizer version, or when a specimen page changed after the gate.
For a document of more than 50 pages the pilot adds five random pages to the specimen. That is the obligatory pilot gate of book-sized documents; the random pages show whether the remedy damages pages that were not defective.
Both commands exit 0 only on PASS. The op pdai:cure_gate reads the exit code and the verdict and publishes a FAIL as an error, so the stage grades FAILED and the Partitur does not reach stage 5.

18.2 Rules

A lesson is an audit rule, a normalizer rule, a layer assignment, an overlay version or an adjudication. A page XML edited by hand is not a lesson; the next production run would reproduce the defect.
An adjudication records that a flag is a validator false positive for the page’s current XML. It is limited to zone and partial codes (FN-IN-BODY, BODY-IN-FN, FN-PARTIAL, FN-MISSING, TXT-GAP, SEG-ORDER); text loss cannot be adjudicated away.
An A/B run whose sample already scores the maximum records improved: false. Such a run is not evidence for or against a model.
Golden queries on the repaired pages are the acceptance criteria for query use.

section: 20.3 Findings and the rules they produced
text:
20.3 Findings and the rules they produced

20.3.1 A tool that reports success while it loses a language
After an upgrade to Stanza 1.12.0 the model cache lacked the Latin proiel tokenizer and the French model. The page parser skipped the sentences of these languages and reported every page as processed, with 0 failures. The corpus fell to 46,515 sentences; GW-II, a Latin edition, had 0 Latin sentences. After the models were restored the corpus held 79,908 sentences, GW-II 6,938 Latin ones. Before the defect was found, the corpus had been rebuilt twice in full, without a test on a few documents.
Rule: the downstream update passes a language gate (a language with at least 100 sentences before the run must not lose more than 5 % of them), and a rebuild of the whole corpus is not a test.


20.3.2 Modification time is not a change
The normalizer writes a stamp into every page it inspects. The downstream stages compared modification times, so every page counted as changed, and the incremental update became a full one. The stages now compare the hash of the page text (text_sha256).
Rule: change detection is by content.


20.3.3 warn can hide a loss
The earlier version of Copernicus1873 page 100 (qwen3.5:cloud) held two of the three note paragraphs of the page: the 46-word paragraph “Für den »burggrabius castri« …” was missing, and the print markers * and ** were numbered 1 and 2. A lost note paragraph falls under FN-PARTIAL or TXT-GAP, which are warn-level codes; a collection can be valid while such losses remain. The current version (qwen3.8:27b-mlx) holds all three paragraphs.
Rule: the diagnosis lists warn pages by code, and codes that stand for lost text are remedied like failures.


20.3.4 An engine that invents a page
GW-IV page 25 is a blank scan: the Vision reading has 0 tokens. The earlier production version by gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview contained a full page of invented English prose (“The study of the celestial mechanics of the solar system …”); its backups page_025.xml.v0 and .v1 keep the evidence. On GW-II page 236 the structured apparatus contains an entry 25 with a wrong reading, while the copy of the apparatus in the page footer is correct.
Rules: TXT-EXCESS is a severe code; a generation error goes into the fault dossier and the learning loop, not into a hand edit of the page.


20.3.5 A rule tested on the pages that need it
The GW-II normalizer rule for apparatus-only pages was run on the whole document as a dry run before it was applied: 174 pages would change, 3 were rejected (pages 337, 374, 376) because their note keys are letters, which the rule did not expect.
Rule: a normalizer is applied only after its specimen gate passes, and the application rejects every page on which the word sequence would change.


20.3.6 Engine calls on detector false positives
The footnote zone of the validity check comes from Vision geometry alone. Notes in the middle of a page, or set at body leading, produce FN-IN-BODY and BODY-IN-FN flags although the XML is right. Re-OCR of such pages spent engine time without a possible gain. The adjudication register now holds 35 facsimile decisions, 9 of them on GW-V (7 BODY-IN-FN, 2 FN-IN-BODY); each binds to the hash of the page XML and lapses when the page changes.
Rule: before a re-OCR of a zone flag, a facsimile check decides whether the flag is a validator false positive.


20.3.7 No stop criterion
Every step above was followed by another run over the collection or the corpus: the full Stanza rebuilds, full audits after each rule, re-OCR over all pages of a flag class. None of these runs had a page or time budget, and none ended with the decision “no improvement, report”.
Rule: one defect class per iteration, 3–5 specimen pages before any application, a page and time budget per iteration, and a report instead of another run when the metric does not improve (see the cure method).

title: 21  Universal letter DTD
text:
21.1 Purpose
Four collections contain letters: the Pirckheimer Briefwechsel (pirckheimer), the letter volumes 13–16 of the Kepler Gesammelte Werke (kepler-prim), the Euler correspondence volumes of series IVA (eulerOO-IVA) and the Kármán archive (karman-nachlass). Each was transcribed under its own page grammar. A query about the sender, the date or the closing of a letter therefore needed one reader per collection. The universal letter DTD page_letter.dtd (v4.2 since 2026-09-28; pdai/pipeline/ai-scholar/src/ai_scholar/schemas/) is one page grammar that holds every letter convention attested in these editions. It is a wrapper of the canonical page.dtd v4.0: margins, meta, figures, tables, p, hi, fn and footnotes come from the page language (Chapter 2), and this file adds the letter families. v4.1 added the diplomatic marks del / add.

A page holds its content in main. A letter’s share of the page is one letter-part; a page on which two letters meet holds two.







Element

21.9 Viewer
The viewer renders the letter elements through the book-sheet renderer window.ReproXML (config/scripts/repro-xml.js; xmlToStructuredHtml in viewer.html is only its fallback), which sets data-el and data-<attr> on each element; the collection’s page.css styles them by [data-el="…"] selectors only and takes its colours from the variables of pdai-page.css, so that the light and the dark scheme both stay legible. letter-ref is not displayed; it is navigation data. The letter-head handler renders the head’s reference chips and then every further child in document order.
